source_title: danielalves96/gow-pc-port: Unofficial native PC port of God of War (2005, PS2) for Windows, with experimental Linux support. Statically recompiled to C++, not an emulator. OpenGL renderer, launcher, cheat menu, widescreen, 60 FPS. Bring your own game d - GitHub
source_excerpt:
God of War (PlayStation 2, NTSC-U SCUS-97399 ) statically recompiled into native C++, for Windows and, experimentally, Linux.
Download: the program is on the Releases page . Get the latest release : on Windows the installer ( ..._x64-setup.exe ) or the portable zip, on Linux the .deb or the AppImage. The green Code button (and "Source code" in a release) only gives you the sources, with no installer: that is for building it yourself. You also need your own copy of the game, see Installing .
This is not an emulator. It is a static recompilation (recomp) : the game's MIPS executable is translated to C++ ahead of time and compiled into a native program. There is no MIPS interpreter, no emulated PS2 hardware and no BIOS at run time. docs/dev/ARCHITECTURE.md shows where that line falls.
This repository ships no game data. No ISO, no SCUS_973.99 , no IRX modules, no .PAK files and no code generated from them. You need your own legal copy of the USA release of God of War for the PlayStation 2 ( SCUS-97399 ). The installer builds everything on your machine from your own disc, and nothing derived from the game ever leaves it.
Static recompilation, not emulation. A recompiler written in Rust translates the game's MIPS code to C++ , which is then compiled into a normal PC program. The PlayStation 2 hardware around it (graphics synthesizer, vector unit, I/O processor, sound, pad, memory card) is implemented natively. Nothing interprets the game's code at run time.
On top of that you get the original 60 Hz game logic, an OpenGL renderer with 1×–6× internal resolution, native movies with sound, a launcher with settings, keyboard and mouse support, a cheat menu, target lock, widescreen, custom texture packs and RetroAchievements.
What that means in practice: the game's own code and the hardware around it are compiled C++ , not something replayed. There are no emulation accuracy hacks here (frame hacks, cycle hacks, per-game patches). The port runs the game's own recompiled code and replaces the libraries that code calls with native ones.
Native renderer : OpenGL 4.6, GPU render targets, internal resolution 1×–6×, bicubic (with sharpening), bilinear or pixel upscaling, FXAA, 480p progressive mode.
Widescreen (Hor+) : 16:9, 16:10 and 21:9 using PCSX2's patch. Switch it off for the game's original 4:3.
Movies : MPEG-2 decoded natively, with sound, including the game's own widescreen versions.
Controls : remappable keyboard and mouse, any gamepad, PS2 or modern layout, per-button swaps, vibration on Windows.
Quality of life : cheat menu ( F2 , nine cheats), target lock ( Alt ), agile combat, FPS counter, fullscreen.
Saves : a PCSX2-compatible Mcd001.ps2 memory card. Cards move between the two in either direction.
Custom textures : PCSX2 replacement packs work, and the launcher can download the community pack.
RetroAchievements : sign-in, in-game notifications and a hardcore mode that disables cheats.
Launcher : eight tabs, a setup wizard, background optimization, English and Brazilian Portuguese.
Linux is experimental. The Linux path is in the repository ( install.sh , the GLFW/GL presentation path, run_gow.sh , the .deb /AppImage packaging), but it hasn't been validated to the same level: no CI job builds or tests the runtime on any platform, the launcher's setup wizard drives install.sh on Linux but has never run on a real Linux machine, vibration is missing, and recent Linux builds haven't been measured. Treat it as prepared, not supported. docs/STATUS.md has the details, area by area.
Why the build is slow and big, and why the PS2 is hard
Your own God of War (USA, SCUS-97399 ) ISO , about 8 GB.
64-bit x86 CPU , 4 cores or more recommended. AVX2 is not required.
OpenGL 4.6 GPU (any recent NVIDIA/AMD, or a recent Intel/AMD iGPU).
8 GB RAM (16 GB while building is comfortable).
Windows 10/11 x64 or a recent Linux (Arch/CachyOS, Ubuntu 24.04+, Fedora 40+); Linux is experimental.
Windows: the launcher. Download the installer from the Releases page, run it, and let the setup wizard do the work. It finds and verifies your ISO, downloads the C++ build tools if they're missing, extracts the disc, recompiles the game and builds it. Then press PLAY .
Windows may warn about an "unknown publisher". The launcher's installer is not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC". Click More info , then Run anyway . The installer contains no game files and its sources are in this repository.
Prefer not to run an installer? The same release has a portable zip ( ..._x64-portable.zip ): unzip it, open God Of War - PC Launcher.exe and the wizard does the rest. Unblock the zip before unzipping (right-click, Properties, Unblock) or Windows shows the same warning for the .exe . It needs the WebView2 runtime, which Windows 11 and updated Windows 10 already have. Every release also lists the SHA-256 of its files in SHA256SUMS-*.txt .
The script checks for CMake, Ninja, a C++ compiler, Git and the GL, X11, Wayland and ALSA development files, and for disk space (30 GB) and RAM (4 GB at least, 8 GB recommended) before it starts. On Arch, Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora (and relatives) --install-deps installs what is missing through sudo ; without the flag it asks in a terminal and otherwise prints the command. On any other distribution it lists what to install. Rust is not needed when the launcher's kit supplies the tools. The launcher's setup wizard does the same on Linux, but you run the package command yourself, because it needs your password.
Both installers accept options (prebuilt tools, destination folder, job count, optimization). Every flag is in docs/INSTALL.md .
The first build compiles about 6,400 generated C++ files. Later updates only rebuild what changed.
Keyboard and mouse work out of the box and are fully remappable in the launcher:
Gamepads (DualShock, DualSense, Xbox, 8BitDo) are plug and play; vibration works on Windows. Saves go to an Mcd001.ps2 memory-card image next to the executable, which is PCSX2-compatible in both directions .
Everything else (the full cheat list, target lock rules, agile combat, memory card details, achievements) is in docs/PLAYING.md . The launcher's tabs and options are in docs/LAUNCHER.md .
The game's logic is tied to the PS2's 60 Hz VBlank, so the game never runs above 60 FPS and never slows down: late frames are dropped. The window can present at 60, 120 or 144 Hz for lower latency.
Internal resolution 2× is the sweet spot. 3× and above are heavy and, on mid-range cards, can stall the presentation.
The CPU side is dominated by the VU1 (the vector unit). Every optimization pass converts more of it to native code: run install.cmd -Optimize / ./install.sh --optimize after playing new areas, or let the launcher's background optimization finish.
A laptop power-saving profile can halve the frame rate , because it clocks down the CPU the VU1 thread needs.
Measured reference points and the tuning order are in docs/PERFORMANCE.md .
Generated code, the extracted disc and the build live in game/ , build-gen/ , build/ and vu1_captures/ , all of which Git ignores.
Two different programs are involved, and they never run at the same time:
At run time the game's own code is ordinary C++: no MIPS interpreter and no emulator sit in the hot path . Around it, a runtime does the PS2 hardware's job: the GS renders with OpenGL, the VU1 runs microcode compiled ahead of time, the IOP runs the game's own IRX modules as native code, and sound, pad and memory card are host services.
The recompiler reproduces PS2Recomp 's output byte for byte; the C++ runtime is built on Waffle565's God-Of-War-Native-Port , with the OpenGL GS backend from the SotC fork of PS2Recomp, and PCSX2 used as the hardware reference. Architecture, build options and testing are in docs/dev/ .
Why the build is slow and big, and why the PS2 is hard
The numbers in What you need (30–90 minutes, ~30 GB) are not padding. They follow from what the installer does and from the machine being ported.
The recompiler turns about 6,400 game functions into about 6,400 C++ files, roughly 129 MB of source . Every MIPS instruction becomes explicit C++ (register access, memory access, branch delay slots, 128-bit multimedia operations), so a few bytes of machine code become many lines. The compiler then optimizes all of it in Release mode, from scratch, once. That is the size of a large application, not of a small project.
The VU1 (the vector unit) runs microcode that is generated ahead of time as native blocks and compiled too. Without that step the game would interpret VU1 code and run much slower.
Parallelism is limited by memory, not only by cores: the installers start at most one compiler process per 2 GB of RAM and cap the VU1 generator at 4 GB by default. A machine with many cores and little RAM builds slowly on purpose, instead of running out of memory.
Changing a header that the generated code includes, or any CMakeLists.txt , rebuilds everything (the precompiled header is regenerated). Later updates rebuild only what changed.
The final game is small next to its build. The space goes mostly to what is needed while installing: your ISO (about 8 GB), the extracted disc (about 8 GB), the Visual Studio Build Tools if they are missing (about 6 GB, Windows), the 129 MB of generated C++, and the object files, precompiled header, VU1 blocks and executables of the build (a few more GB). That adds up to roughly 25 GB, and the requirement leaves headroom on top. It is a safe margin, not a measured size.

That is why this port needs a recompiler, a native GS, a VU1 generator, an IOP layer and a lot of captured data, and not just a translator for one CPU. It is also why the installer cannot ship a ready-made binary: it would contain the game's code, which this repository never distributes (see License and legal ).
Contributions are welcome: bug reports (with a log), fixes and documentation. Read docs/dev/README.md and docs/dev/BUILD.md first. The short version:
Rust builds the tools, C++ runs the game. Never edit generated files by hand.
Changes to code taken from the upstream projects carry a // GOW-Port: comment.
cargo test --workspace must pass, cargo clippy … -D warnings must stay clean, and the parity gate must stay byte-identical.
Never commit anything derived from the game.
This port stands on other people's work, above all PS2Recomp , KIexster's God of War recompilation , Waffle565's native port and PCSX2 . The full inventory, including what comes from where and under which license, is in docs/THIRD_PARTY.md .
The code in this repository is GPL-3.0 (see LICENSE ), like the projects it builds on. Vendored libraries keep their own licenses, listed in docs/THIRD_PARTY.md .

Unofficial native PC port of God of War (2005, PS2) for Windows, with experimental Linux support. Statically recompiled to C++, not an emulator. OpenGL renderer, launcher, cheat menu, widescreen, 60 FPS. Bring your own game dump: no game files included.
